title: Hashing, sharding & partitioning math
description: What sharding COSTS once you know how many shards you need (02-caching-and-pools/06-shard-count covers that count): keys moved under modulo versus consistent hashing, the load each survivor absorbs when a node dies, hot-key skew, the copy time of a rebalance, partition pruning on time ranges, weighted vnodes, scatter-gather amplification, and why partitions cap consumer parallelism. Uniform key distribution is assumed and stated, shares are in per-mille (parts per thousand) and copy rates in decimal units (1 MB/s = 1,000,000 bytes/s), so every answer is a whole number.

exercises.title: Keys moved: modulo vs consistent hashing
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We cache 1,000,000 keys on 4 nodes using `hash(key) % 4`. Traffic grew, so we add a fifth node. How many keys now map to a different node — and how many would move with consistent hashing?"

**Why it works.** Model: keys are spread uniformly over a span divisible by n × (n + 1). Under `key % shards` a key stays put only when its remainder mod n equals its remainder mod (n + 1), which happens for exactly **1 key in every (n + 1)**. So n ÷ (n + 1) of all keys move — 80% going from 4 to 5 nodes, which means a cache stampede and a rebalance storm. Consistent hashing places nodes on a ring: the new node takes over only its own 1 ÷ (n + 1) slice from its neighbours, and nothing else moves.

**Your task.** Export two functions (`oldShards` is n, the count before adding one):
- `movedKeysModulo(totalKeys, oldShards)` → `totalKeys × oldShards / (oldShards + 1)`
- `movedKeysConsistent(totalKeys, oldShards)` → `totalKeys / (oldShards + 1)` (only the new node's share moves)

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 600,000 keys going from 2 nodes to 3: modulo moves 600,000 × 2 / 3 = **400,000** keys; consistent hashing moves 600,000 / 3 = **200,000**.

tests.name: modulo, 4 -> 5 shards: 800,000 of 1,000,000 keys move
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.movedKeysModulo, 'function', 'export a function named movedKeysModulo');
assert.equal(mod.movedKeysModulo(1000000, 4), 800000);

tests.name: modulo, 2 -> 3 shards: 400,000 of 600,000 keys move
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.movedKeysModulo, 'function', 'export a function named movedKeysModulo');
assert.equal(mod.movedKeysModulo(600000, 2), 400000);

tests.name: consistent, 4 -> 5 nodes: 200,000 keys move
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.movedKeysConsistent, 'function', 'export a function named movedKeysConsistent');
assert.equal(mod.movedKeysConsistent(1000000, 4), 200000);

tests.name: consistent, 2 -> 3 nodes: 200,000 keys move
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.movedKeysConsistent, 'function', 'export a function named movedKeysConsistent');
assert.equal(mod.movedKeysConsistent(600000, 2), 200000);

tests.name: modulo, even 1 -> 2 shards moves half (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.movedKeysModulo, 'function', 'export a function named movedKeysModulo');
assert.equal(mod.movedKeysModulo(1000000, 1), 500000);

exercises.explanation:
Count the keys that keep their node; everything else moves.

For `movedKeysModulo(1000000, 4)` versus `movedKeysConsistent(1000000, 4)`:
- modulo: only 1 key in 5 keeps its remainder, so 1,000,000 × 4 / 5 = **800,000** keys move (80%)
- consistent: the new node takes its 1 / 5 share, so 1,000,000 / 5 = **200,000** keys move (20%)

Under modulo, 80% of cache lookups miss at once and stampede the database while 80% of stored data copies — consistent hashing moves exactly the 20% the new node owns, which is the whole reason it exists.
hints: A key stays on its node only if its old and new shard numbers agree — how often does key % n equal key % (n + 1)?
Modulo: moved = total × n / (n + 1). Consistent: moved = total / (n + 1).
Under modulo only 1 key in (old + 1) keeps its remainder, so old ÷ (old + 1) of them move. Consistent hashing relocates only the newcomer's 1 ÷ (old + 1) share.

exercises.title: When a node dies: load on the survivors
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "12,000,000 keys live on 4 cache nodes using consistent hashing with many virtual nodes. One node dies. How many keys does each survivor hold now?"

**Why it works.** With many vnodes per box, a dead node's ring slices are scattered all over the ring, so its keys spread evenly across every survivor instead of landing on one neighbour. Each survivor goes from total ÷ n keys to total ÷ (n − 1). Survivors need that headroom in advance — capacity is sized for n − 1 nodes, not n.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `keysPerNode(totalKeys, nodes)` → `totalKeys / nodes`
- `keysPerSurvivor(totalKeys, nodes)` → `totalKeys / (nodes - 1)` (one of `nodes` has died, nodes ≥ 2)

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 60,000,000 keys on 5 nodes → 12,000,000 each; lose one → 60,000,000 / 4 = **15,000,000** per survivor (+25%).

tests.name: 12M keys on 4 nodes -> 3,000,000 each
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysPerNode, 'function', 'export a function named keysPerNode');
assert.equal(mod.keysPerNode(12000000, 4), 3000000);

tests.name: 4 nodes lose one -> 4,000,000 per survivor (+33%)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysPerSurvivor, 'function', 'export a function named keysPerSurvivor');
assert.equal(mod.keysPerSurvivor(12000000, 4), 4000000);

tests.name: 60M keys on 5 nodes -> 12,000,000 each
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysPerNode, 'function', 'export a function named keysPerNode');
assert.equal(mod.keysPerNode(60000000, 5), 12000000);

tests.name: 5 nodes lose one -> 15,000,000 per survivor (+25%)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysPerSurvivor, 'function', 'export a function named keysPerSurvivor');
assert.equal(mod.keysPerSurvivor(60000000, 5), 15000000);

tests.name: 2 nodes lose one -> the survivor takes everything (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysPerSurvivor, 'function', 'export a function named keysPerSurvivor');
assert.equal(mod.keysPerSurvivor(10000000, 2), 10000000);

exercises.explanation:
Same keys, one fewer node: compare the two even splits.

For `keysPerSurvivor(12000000, 4)`:
- before: 12,000,000 / 4 = 3,000,000 keys per node
- after: 12,000,000 / 3 = **4,000,000** keys per survivor
- surge: +1,000,000 each, +33%

If every node normally runs above 75% of its memory or CPU, losing one pushes the survivors past 100% and the failure cascades — which is why you size for n − 1, not n.
hints: With many vnodes, a dead node's keys are scattered across every survivor, not dumped on one neighbour.
before = total / nodes. after = total / (nodes − 1).
After a loss the same keys divide among one fewer node — compare total ÷ nodes with total ÷ (nodes − 1) to see the surge each survivor absorbs.

exercises.title: Hot-key skew on one shard
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "100,000 QPS hits 10 shards. One celebrity account gets 20% of all traffic. How loaded is that account's shard compared with a fair share?"

**Why it works.** Hashing spreads **keys**, not requests. One key always lands on one shard, so that shard carries the hot key's entire traffic plus its even slice of everything else. The fair share is total ÷ shards; skew in per-mille compares the hot shard with it (1,000‰ = perfectly even, 2,000‰ = twice the fair share). Shares are given in per-mille: 200‰ = 20%.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `hotShardQps(totalQps, shards, hotKeyPermille)` → `totalQps × hotKeyPermille / 1000 + totalQps × (1000 - hotKeyPermille) / 1000 / shards`
- `skewPermille(totalQps, shards, hotKeyPermille)` → `hotShardQps(...) × 1000 / (totalQps / shards)` (the hot shard as per-mille of the fair share)

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 50,000 QPS, 5 shards, a 400‰ hot key: the hot key brings 20,000 QPS, the rest is 30,000 / 5 = 6,000 per shard, so the hot shard runs **26,000 QPS** against a fair share of 10,000.

tests.name: 100,000 QPS, 10 shards, 200 per-mille hot key -> 28,000 QPS
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.hotShardQps, 'function', 'export a function named hotShardQps');
assert.equal(mod.hotShardQps(100000, 10, 200), 28000);

tests.name: no hot key -> exactly the fair share (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.hotShardQps, 'function', 'export a function named hotShardQps');
assert.equal(mod.hotShardQps(100000, 10, 0), 10000);

tests.name: 50,000 QPS, 5 shards, 400 per-mille hot key -> 26,000 QPS
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.hotShardQps, 'function', 'export a function named hotShardQps');
assert.equal(mod.hotShardQps(50000, 5, 400), 26000);

tests.name: hot shard at 2,800 per-mille of fair share (2.8x)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.skewPermille, 'function', 'export a function named skewPermille');
assert.equal(mod.skewPermille(100000, 10, 200), 2800);

tests.name: hot shard at 2,600 per-mille of fair share (2.6x)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.skewPermille, 'function', 'export a function named skewPermille');
assert.equal(mod.skewPermille(50000, 5, 400), 2600);

exercises.explanation:
Build the hot shard's load from its two parts, then compare it with the fair share.

For `skewPermille(100000, 10, 200)`:
- hot key: 100,000 × 200 / 1,000 = 20,000 QPS
- its slice of the rest: 100,000 × 800 / 1,000 / 10 = 8,000 QPS
- hot shard = 28,000 QPS; fair share = 100,000 / 10 = 10,000 QPS
- skew = 28,000 × 1,000 / 10,000 = **2,800‰** (2.8×)

Adding shards does not fix it — even at 100 shards the hot key's full 20,000 QPS still lands on one of them — so split the key (salt it into sub-keys) or cache it in front.
hints: Hashing spreads keys, not requests — one key, however busy, always lands on a single shard.
hot = total × h / 1000 + total × (1000 − h) / 1000 / shards. skew‰ = hot × 1000 / (total / shards).
The hot shard carries the whole hot key plus its even slice of the remaining traffic. Divide by the fair share (total ÷ shards) and scale to per-mille for the skew.

exercises.title: Rebalance: bytes to move and copy time
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A 9 TB dataset lives on 2 shards placed by consistent hashing. We add a third. How much data moves, and how long does the copy take at 150 MB/s?"

**Why it works.** With consistent hashing, growing from `oldShards` to `newShards` hands the new shards their share and nothing else moves: the (new − old) ÷ new fraction of the data. Copy time is bytes ÷ rate, in decimal units: 1 MB/s = 1,000,000 bytes/s and 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `bytesToMove(totalBytes, oldShards, newShards)` → `totalBytes × (newShards - oldShards) / newShards`
- `rebalanceSeconds(bytesToMove, mbPerSec)` → `bytesToMove / (mbPerSec × 1000000)`

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 8 TB going from 4 to 8 shards: 8,000,000,000,000 × 4 / 8 = 4,000,000,000,000 bytes (half); at 200 MB/s that is 4,000,000,000,000 / 200,000,000 = **20,000 s**.

tests.name: 9 TB, 2 -> 3 shards: a third (3 TB) moves
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.bytesToMove, 'function', 'export a function named bytesToMove');
assert.equal(mod.bytesToMove(9000000000000, 2, 3), 3000000000000);

tests.name: 8 TB, 4 -> 8 shards: doubling moves half
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.bytesToMove, 'function', 'export a function named bytesToMove');
assert.equal(mod.bytesToMove(8000000000000, 4, 8), 4000000000000);

tests.name: no change in shard count -> nothing moves (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.bytesToMove, 'function', 'export a function named bytesToMove');
assert.equal(mod.bytesToMove(5000000000000, 5, 5), 0);

tests.name: 3 TB at 150 MB/s -> 20,000 s (about 5.5 hours)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rebalanceSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named rebalanceSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.rebalanceSeconds(3000000000000, 150), 20000);

tests.name: 4 TB at 200 MB/s -> 20,000 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rebalanceSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named rebalanceSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.rebalanceSeconds(4000000000000, 200), 20000);

exercises.explanation:
Find the fraction that moves, then divide by the copy rate in bytes per second.

For the 9 TB, 2 → 3 shard case at 150 MB/s:
- moved = 9,000,000,000,000 × (3 − 2) / 3 = 3,000,000,000,000 bytes (3 TB)
- rate = 150 × 1,000,000 = 150,000,000 bytes/s
- time = `rebalanceSeconds(3000000000000, 150)` = 3,000,000,000,000 / 150,000,000 = **20,000 s** (about 5.5 hours)

Hours of sustained copy traffic is why rebalances are planned operations, not clicks — throttle the copy or it starves production I/O.
hints: Consistent hashing only hands the new shards their share — the old shards keep everything else.
moved = total × (new − old) / new. seconds = moved / (MB/s × 1,000,000).
Growing old → new moves the (new − old) ÷ new fraction of the data. Divide bytes moved by the copy rate in bytes per second (MB/s × one million).

exercises.title: Partition pruning on time ranges
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "An events table is range-partitioned by week (7-day partitions) with 21,000,000 rows per partition. A dashboard queries the last 30 days. How many partitions and rows does it scan?"

**Why it works.** With range partitioning, the planner **prunes** every partition the `WHERE` clause on the partition key cannot touch. Model: a D-day window over P-day partitions needs D ÷ P partitions **rounded up** — a window that does not fill its last partition exactly still reads that whole partition. (A window that starts mid-partition can straddle one more boundary; this drill uses the simple ceiling.)

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `partitionsScanned(daysQueried, daysPerPartition)` → `Math.ceil(daysQueried / daysPerPartition)`
- `rowsScanned(daysQueried, daysPerPartition, rowsPerPartition)` → `partitionsScanned(...) × rowsPerPartition`

**Worked example.** 28 days of weekly partitions → exactly **4** partitions; 30 days → 30 / 7 ≈ 4.3, rounded up to **5**.

tests.name: 30 days over 7-day partitions -> 5
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.partitionsScanned, 'function', 'export a function named partitionsScanned');
assert.equal(mod.partitionsScanned(30, 7), 5);

tests.name: 28 days over 7-day partitions -> exact fit, 4 (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.partitionsScanned, 'function', 'export a function named partitionsScanned');
assert.equal(mod.partitionsScanned(28, 7), 4);

tests.name: 1 day -> still one whole partition
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.partitionsScanned, 'function', 'export a function named partitionsScanned');
assert.equal(mod.partitionsScanned(1, 7), 1);

tests.name: 30 days, weekly partitions of 21M rows -> 105,000,000 rows
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rowsScanned, 'function', 'export a function named rowsScanned');
assert.equal(mod.rowsScanned(30, 7, 21000000), 105000000);

tests.name: 1 day over daily partitions of 3M rows -> 3,000,000 rows
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rowsScanned, 'function', 'export a function named rowsScanned');
assert.equal(mod.rowsScanned(1, 1, 3000000), 3000000);

exercises.explanation:
Count the partitions the window touches (rounding up), then multiply by rows per partition.

For `rowsScanned(30, 7, 21000000)`:
- partitions = ⌈30 / 7⌉ = ⌈4.29⌉ = 5
- rows = 5 × 21,000,000 = **105,000,000**

A year of weekly partitions is 52 × 21,000,000 ≈ 1.1 billion rows, so pruning reads about a tenth of the table — but only for queries that filter on the partition key; without it, every partition is scanned.
hints: The planner reads only the partitions the time range can touch and skips the rest.
partitions = ⌈daysQueried / daysPerPartition⌉. rows = partitions × rowsPerPartition.
A span of D days over P-day partitions can straddle a boundary, so round D ÷ P UP. Multiply by each partition's rows for the scan size.

exercises.title: Weighted vnodes: keys follow ownership
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our hash ring has 300 vnodes over 48,000,000 keys. A big box owns 75 vnodes and a small one owns 25. How many keys does each hold? And how many vnodes should a node get for a 25% share of a 400-vnode ring?"

**Why it works.** In consistent hashing each physical node owns many **virtual nodes** (points on the ring). With enough vnodes, a node's share of the keys equals its share of the vnodes, so bigger boxes simply get proportionally more vnodes. Shares are given in per-mille: 250‰ = 25%.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `keysForNode(totalKeys, totalVnodes, nodeVnodes)` → `totalKeys × nodeVnodes / totalVnodes`
- `vnodesForShare(totalVnodes, sharePermille)` → `totalVnodes × sharePermille / 1000`

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 75 of 300 vnodes → 48,000,000 × 75 / 300 = **12,000,000 keys** (a quarter of the ring).

tests.name: 75 of 300 vnodes over 48M keys -> 12,000,000 keys
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysForNode, 'function', 'export a function named keysForNode');
assert.equal(mod.keysForNode(48000000, 300, 75), 12000000);

tests.name: a third the vnodes -> a third the keys: 4,000,000
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysForNode, 'function', 'export a function named keysForNode');
assert.equal(mod.keysForNode(48000000, 300, 25), 4000000);

tests.name: drained node with 0 vnodes -> 0 keys (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.keysForNode, 'function', 'export a function named keysForNode');
assert.equal(mod.keysForNode(10000000, 100, 0), 0);

tests.name: 250 per-mille of a 400-vnode ring -> 100 vnodes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.vnodesForShare, 'function', 'export a function named vnodesForShare');
assert.equal(mod.vnodesForShare(400, 250), 100);

tests.name: 125 per-mille of a 640-vnode ring -> 80 vnodes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.vnodesForShare, 'function', 'export a function named vnodesForShare');
assert.equal(mod.vnodesForShare(640, 125), 80);

exercises.explanation:
A node's key share is its vnode share; invert that to choose a vnode count.

For `vnodesForShare(640, 125)`:
- 640 × 125 = 80,000
- 80,000 / 1,000 = **80 vnodes** (12.5% of the ring)

Vnodes are the knob — to drain a node for maintenance, walk its vnode count down to zero and its keys follow a slice at a time.
hints: With many vnodes, each node's share of the keys matches its share of the ring's vnodes.
keys = totalKeys × nodeVnodes / totalVnodes. vnodes = totalVnodes × share‰ / 1000.
Keys distribute in proportion to vnode ownership: the node's share is its vnodes over the ring's total. Invert to pick a vnode count for a target per-mille share.

exercises.title: Scatter-gather amplification
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our API serves 2,000 QPS over 8 shards. Calls that include the tenant id route to one shard; the rest must ask all 8 and merge. If 75% of calls carry the key, how many shard queries per second hit the backend?"

**Why it works.** A keyed call costs **one** shard query. An unkeyed call must scatter to **every** shard and gather the results, so it costs `shards` queries (and waits for the slowest shard). Blend the two populations by per-mille share: per 1,000 API calls the backend sees keyed‰ × 1 + (1000 − keyed‰) × shards queries. The worst case — nothing keyed — is apiQps × shards.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `shardQueriesPerSec(apiQps, shards, keyedPermille)` → `apiQps × (keyedPermille × 1 + (1000 - keyedPermille) × shards) / 1000`
- `queriesSavedPerSec(apiQps, shards, keyedPermille)` → `apiQps × shards - shardQueriesPerSec(...)` (saved versus every call fanning out)

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 4,000 QPS, 16 shards, 900‰ keyed: per 1,000 calls 900 × 1 + 100 × 16 = 2,500 shard queries → 4,000 × 2,500 / 1,000 = **10,000 shard queries/s**.

tests.name: every call keyed -> 2,000 shard queries/s (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.shardQueriesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named shardQueriesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.shardQueriesPerSec(2000, 8, 1000), 2000);

tests.name: nothing keyed -> full fan-out, 16,000/s (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.shardQueriesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named shardQueriesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.shardQueriesPerSec(2000, 8, 0), 16000);

tests.name: 750 per-mille keyed over 8 shards -> 5,500/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.shardQueriesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named shardQueriesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.shardQueriesPerSec(2000, 8, 750), 5500);

tests.name: 750 per-mille keyed saves 10,500 shard queries/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.queriesSavedPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named queriesSavedPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.queriesSavedPerSec(2000, 8, 750), 10500);

tests.name: 4,000 QPS, 16 shards, 900 per-mille keyed -> 10,000/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.shardQueriesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named shardQueriesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.shardQueriesPerSec(4000, 16, 900), 10000);

exercises.explanation:
Price each population, blend by per-mille share, and compare with the all-fan-out worst case.

For `shardQueriesPerSec(2000, 8, 750)`:
- per 1,000 calls: 750 × 1 + 250 × 8 = 750 + 2,000 = 2,750 shard queries
- per second: 2,000 × 2,750 / 1,000 = **5,500**
- saved versus full fan-out: 2,000 × 8 − 5,500 = 16,000 − 5,500 = 10,500

The unkeyed 25% of callers still generate 4,000 of those 5,500 shard queries (about 73%) — which is why APIs force the tenant id into the path.
hints: There are two kinds of calls: ones that know their shard, and ones that must ask every shard.
per-1000 cost = keyed‰ × 1 + (1000 − keyed‰) × shards. shard QPS = apiQps × that / 1000. saved = apiQps × shards − shard QPS.
Weight the two populations: keyed calls cost one shard query, unkeyed cost one per shard. Blend by per-mille share and compare with the all-fan-out worst case.

exercises.title: Partitions cap consumer parallelism
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A Kafka topic has 12 partitions. We run 5 consumers in one consumer group, then scale to 20. How many consumers actually do work, and how many partitions does the busiest one own?"

**Why it works.** Within one consumer group, each partition is assigned to **at most one** consumer — that is how per-partition ordering is kept. So active consumers = the smaller of partitions and consumers; any extra consumers sit idle. Partitions are spread as evenly as possible, so the busiest consumer owns partitions ÷ active consumers, **rounded up**.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `activeConsumers(partitions, consumers)` → `Math.min(partitions, consumers)`
- `busiestConsumerPartitions(partitions, consumers)` → `Math.ceil(partitions / Math.min(partitions, consumers))`

**Worked example.** 12 partitions, 5 consumers → 5 active; 12 / 5 = 2.4, rounded up → the busiest consumer owns **3** partitions.

tests.name: 12 partitions, 5 consumers -> 5 active
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.activeConsumers, 'function', 'export a function named activeConsumers');
assert.equal(mod.activeConsumers(12, 5), 5);

tests.name: 12 partitions, 20 consumers -> 12 active, 8 idle (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.activeConsumers, 'function', 'export a function named activeConsumers');
assert.equal(mod.activeConsumers(12, 20), 12);

tests.name: 12 partitions over 5 consumers -> busiest owns 3
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.busiestConsumerPartitions, 'function', 'export a function named busiestConsumerPartitions');
assert.equal(mod.busiestConsumerPartitions(12, 5), 3);

tests.name: 12 partitions over 4 consumers -> even split, 3 each
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.busiestConsumerPartitions, 'function', 'export a function named busiestConsumerPartitions');
assert.equal(mod.busiestConsumerPartitions(12, 4), 3);

tests.name: 12 partitions, 20 consumers -> 1 each
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.busiestConsumerPartitions, 'function', 'export a function named busiestConsumerPartitions');
assert.equal(mod.busiestConsumerPartitions(12, 20), 1);

tests.name: 7 partitions, 7 consumers -> one each (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.busiestConsumerPartitions, 'function', 'export a function named busiestConsumerPartitions');
assert.equal(mod.busiestConsumerPartitions(7, 7), 1);

exercises.explanation:
Cap the active consumers at the partition count, then split the partitions evenly and round up.

For `busiestConsumerPartitions(12, 20)`:
- active = min(12, 20) = 12 (8 consumers sit idle)
- busiest = ⌈12 / 12⌉ = **1** partition

The partition count is the parallelism ceiling and it is chosen at topic creation — scaling consumers past it buys nothing, so pick partitions for the peak consumer count you expect.
hints: Inside one consumer group a partition is read by exactly one consumer — it is never shared.
active = min(partitions, consumers). busiest = ⌈partitions / active⌉.
At most one consumer per partition caps the active count at the smaller of the two. The busiest consumer holds the partition count divided by active consumers, rounded up.
